segments.voice: Yesterday, the night book, Sauptika, ended by the Ganga, and Draupadi took the jewel instead of a life. Your line was kshama: Draupadi takes the jewel, not his life.

segments.voice: A traveler is lost in a thick forest full of wild animals. Running from them, he falls into a well, but he doesn't hit the bottom. Creepers catch him, and he hangs there, upside down. Below him waits a great serpent. Above him, at the well's mouth, stands a dark elephant. Rats are gnawing at the roots of the tree that holds the creepers. And from a honeycomb in the branches, a drop of honey falls toward his mouth. This is how Stri, the book of the women, begins: with Vidura telling a story to a grieving king.
screen: `A MAN HANGS IN A WELL.` → `A SERPENT BELOW.` → `A DROP OF HONEY.`

segments.voice: The war is over. In Hastinapura, the old blind king Dhritarashtra hears that Duryodhana and his brothers are dead, and he falls to the ground in grief. His half-brother Vidura sits with him and tells a story: the man in the well. And what does the man do, hanging between the serpent and the elephant, with the rats chewing the roots? He drinks the honey, and he wants more. Then Vidura explains. The forest is the world we wander in. The wild animals are illnesses. The well is the body. The serpent at the bottom is Time, which takes everything. The elephant is the year; the rats are the days and nights; the creepers are the hope of life that holds us. The honey is the pleasures we keep reaching for, even here. Hindus have a name for this whole picture: samsara, the turning world of birth and death, where Time carries off everything that's born. Vidura is describing everyone, the king included. It's the same truth Krishna gives Arjuna in the Gita: for whoever is born, death is certain, so don't grieve as if it shouldn't have happened. That's why, at a death, you may hear a Hindu family say quietly, it's samsara. It doesn't mean don't be sad. It means this comes to all of us, and nobody is alone in the well.
screen: `THE KING HEARS THE NEWS` · `VIDURA TELLS A STORY` · `THE WELL IS SAMSARA` · then, large: `FOR THE BORN, DEATH IS CERTAIN`

segments.voice: Many Hindus chant the Mahamrityunjaya mantra for the sick and the dying. It asks Shiva for freedom from death's grip, the way a ripe cucumber slips easily from its vine. Sit quietly and picture the man's creepers, then that ripe fruit letting go without a struggle. Breathe in, holding on; breathe out, loosening. If you pray, you can say the mantra, or simply ask to let go well when it's time. If you don't, rest with the picture of the ripe fruit.

856.title: the iron Bhima
856.hook: a blind king asks to embrace the man who killed his sons, and Krishna slides an iron statue into his arms

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stri opened with Vidura's man in the well. Your line was samsara, held by time, still reaching for honey.

segments.voice: A line of chariots and carts leaves Hastinapura, and behind it walk the women of the royal house, weeping, their hair unbound. They're going out to the battlefield to find their dead. At the front is Dhritarashtra, the blind old king, with Gandhari beside him. On the road, the Pandavas come to meet him: the five brothers who won, with Krishna. They bow. The king has to greet them. And he asks for one of them in particular.
screen: `THE WOMEN WALK OUT.` → `THE PANDAVAS COME TO MEET HIM.` → `HE ASKS FOR ONE.`

segments.voice: Dhritarashtra embraces Yudhishthira first, the text says, without joy. Then he asks for Bhima, the one who killed Duryodhana and Duhshasana. Krishna understands what's in the old man's heart. He quietly pushes Bhima aside and moves forward an iron statue of Bhima, which Duryodhana had made, in Ganguli's telling, to practice against with his mace. The blind king takes the iron figure in his arms and crushes it, so strong with grief and rage that it breaks apart, and he hurts himself. He falls, and Sanjaya lifts him up. Then he weeps for Bhima, sure he has killed him. Krishna speaks. It was only an image of iron, he says, in effect. Your sons died by their own deeds, and because you didn't stop them. The king is ashamed, and maybe relieved. He washes, and embraces the brothers, Bhima too, with blessings this time. Hindus have a word for what blinded this king long before today: moha, the love that clings to what's mine until it can't see straight. His eyes were blind from birth, but many teachers say this was his deeper blindness. The Gita opens with his voice asking what my sons and Pandu's sons did, and teachers often point to that one word, my, as the whole war in seed. It ends with Arjuna saying, my moha is gone. Krishna doesn't shame the king. He gives the grief iron to break, then names the truth. Moha isn't too little love. It's love that only sees mine.
screen: `HE ASKS FOR BHIMA` · `AN IRON STATUE INSTEAD` · `"YOUR SONS DIED BY THEIR OWN DEEDS"` · then, large: `MOHA: LOVE THAT ONLY SEES MINE`

segments.voice: At a Hindu fire offering, as each spoonful of ghee goes into the flame, the words are often idam na mama: this is not mine. Make two fists slowly, holding something you love tightly in your mind, a person, a plan, a side you're on. Breathe in and feel the grip. Breathe out and open your hands, palms up, as if setting it into the fire: not mine. If you pray, you can offer that person to God with open hands. If you don't, just let the hands stay open.

segments.voice: The winners of the war have a visit to make, and nobody wants to make it. The five Pandava brothers, with Krishna beside them, have to stand in front of Gandhari, the queen whose sons fell to them on that field. She has kept her eyes bound with a cloth for her whole married life, the story says, and her years of discipline have given her a power the brothers fear. Her anger could burn. Before they arrive, the sage Vyasa comes to her first.
screen: `THE WINNERS MUST VISIT.` → `A MOTHER WITH BOUND EYES.` → `VYASA COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Vyasa reminds Gandhari of her own words. All through the war, when Duryodhana came asking for her blessing, she gave him the same answer: where dharma is, there victory is. She never blessed him with victory. Now, Vyasa says, the words have come true. Don't let anger undo them. So she holds the curse back, but she has a question for Bhima. Why did you strike my son below the navel, against the rules of the mace fight? Bhima admits he was afraid, and reminds her what her son did to Draupadi. Then Gandhari asks for the king. Yudhishthira comes forward, trembling, hands joined: I killed your sons. Curse me. Gandhari says nothing. But through a small gap in the cloth, her gaze falls on the tips of his toes, and his nails turn dark and damaged. Arjuna, watching, steps behind Krishna. Then her anger passes, and she sends them to their own mother, Kunti. One glance, and that's all the burning there is. Now hold on to her words: yato dharmas tato jayah, where dharma is, there is victory. She said them to her own son, and wouldn't bend them for him. Hindus still live by that line; it's the motto of India's Supreme Court. The teaching: you don't bless your own side. You bless what's right, and trust victory to follow it. Today, when someone you love asks you to take their side, that's Gandhari's test.
screen: `WHERE DHARMA IS, THERE IS VICTORY` · `BHIMA ANSWERS HONESTLY` · `ONE GLANCE AT HIS TOES` · then, large: `YATO DHARMAS TATO JAYAH`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, the way Gandhari's were closed, and bring back a moment when someone close to you wanted you on their side, and you could have said the thing that burned. Breathe in and feel the heat; breathe out and rest in the space between the heat and the words. If you pray, you can ask, as Gandhari did, not for your side to win, but for dharma. If you don't, just rest in that space a little longer.

858.carry: the equal eye: their grief as your own

segments.voice: For years Gandhari has lived behind a cloth she tied on herself. Now the sage Vyasa gives her what the text calls a celestial sight, a way to see far beyond where she stands. She doesn't turn it on the sky, or the palace, or the faces of the Pandavas. She turns it on the field of Kurukshetra, where the war just ended. And beside her stands Krishna, the one person she will speak to about all of it.
screen: `A CLOTH SHE TIED HERSELF.` → `VYASA GIVES HER SIGHT.` → `SHE LOOKS AT THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: What she sees first isn't warriors. It's women. Wives, mothers and daughters of both armies move across the field, searching. Some have never walked outside the women's quarters before, and now they're out among the dead, hair loose, calling names. Gandhari describes it all to Krishna, scene after scene. She sees Uttara, the young widow of Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son, bending over him and talking to him as if he could still hear. She sees her own daughter, Duhshala, searching for her husband Jayadratha and unable to find his head. She sees her son Duryodhana on the ground, and his wife beside him. She sees Karna, and the women grieving him too. And she keeps turning to Krishna. Look at this, she says. Look at her. A Pandava widow and a Kaurava widow, doing exactly the same thing in the dust. The war books counted who killed whom. Stri counts who's left to bury them. Many teachers hear in this a teaching of the Gita: the wise look on all with an equal eye, and the highest yogi, measuring by their own heart, feels the joy and sorrow of others as their own. Hindus ground it in the Self: the same atman lives in every being, so the same grief lives in every widow. Gandhari, the Kaurava mother, doesn't stop at her own. Today, when the news counts only one side's dead, she's the one saying, look at her too.
screen: `SHE SEES THE WOMEN FIRST` · `UTTARA, DUHSHALA, DURYODHANA'S WIFE` · `GRIEF FROM BOTH CAMPS` · then, large: `THE EQUAL EYE`

segments.voice: Many Hindus end their prayers with sarve bhavantu sukhinah: may all be happy, may all be free from illness. Let your eyes rest soft, and bring to mind a conflict you know, near or far, in your family or in the news. Set aside the people who fought it, and let one person left behind on each side come into view, one with the in-breath, one with the out-breath. Then say it for both: may all be happy. If you don't pray, just hold them side by side.

segments.voice: She has been talking to Krishna the whole time. Look at this widow, look at that mother, look at my son. And somewhere in that long walk across the field, the grief turns. Gandhari stops describing and starts accusing. You could have stopped this, she tells him. You had the power. You had the words. Both sides listened to you, and you let it happen. The curse in this book's title isn't aimed at the Pandavas. It's aimed at Krishna, standing right beside her.
screen: `THE GRIEF TURNS.` → `"YOU COULD HAVE STOPPED THIS."` → `THE CURSE IS FOR KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Gandhari reaches for the power her discipline has given her, the power she held back with Yudhishthira. Because you stood by while the Kurus and the Pandavas destroyed each other, she says, your own kinsmen, the Vrishnis, will kill one another. You yourself will die alone, in a wild place, by an inglorious means. And the women of your house will weep over their dead, the way the women of mine are weeping now. Krishna doesn't argue or defend the war. In Ganguli's telling he answers calmly, almost with a smile. I already knew this, he says, in effect. My people can be destroyed by no one but themselves. Then he gently turns her grief back to her. The war came, he says, from your son's choices, and from your own failure to restrain him. Get up. Don't give yourself to sorrow. Gandhari falls silent. So the curse lands, and Krishna accepts it. The book doesn't settle whether she was right to blame him. But many teachers see Krishna here living what he taught Arjuna on this same field: the sthitaprajna, the one of steady wisdom, whose mind isn't shaken in sorrow, who is free of craving, fear and anger. And Hindu devotion makes room for Gandhari too. A grieving mother says something almost unsayable to Krishna, whom the epic honors as God, and he takes it without striking back. Today, when someone's grief comes at you as blame, steady isn't cold.

segments.voice: Water is the last thing the living can give the dead. After the fires on the field are lit, the whole household walks down to the Ganga: the Pandavas, Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti, the widows of both sides. One by one they step into the river and offer water for each person they lost, a father, a brother, a son, a teacher. A quiet, orderly rite after so much noise. And in the middle of it, Kunti tells her sons something she has carried their whole lives.
screen: `THE FIRES ARE LIT.` → `EVERYONE GOES TO THE GANGA.` → `KUNTI SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Kunti asks her sons to offer water for one more warrior: Karna. The brothers are puzzled. Karna was the enemy, the charioteer's son, the man Arjuna killed. Why him? He was your eldest brother, Kunti tells them. My son, born to me from the sun god before I married your father. I set him adrift as a baby, and I never told you. The Pandavas are stunned. Yudhishthira is crushed. Soon after, as the next book opens, he remembers how Karna's feet resembled Kunti's, and how his anger used to drain away when he looked at them. Now he understands why. He offers the water for Karna himself, and brings Karna's family into the rites. This is a rite Hindus still keep. It's called tarpan: water poured from cupped hands for the ones who have died, often standing in a river, often with sesame seeds, naming each one. Families offer it after a death, and again every year, especially in Pitru Paksha, the fortnight for the ancestors. The teaching underneath: the living owe the dead remembrance, and nobody belongs off the list. Karna was left off until a woman spoke. So Stri ends at the river. The women speak, and the winners learn what their victory cost. Today, think of who's missing from your own list: the relative nobody mentions, the friend you lost touch with.

segments.voice: Yudhishthira has everything he fought for, and he doesn't want any of it. The kingdom is his. His enemies are gone. And he tells his brothers he's leaving for the forest, to live as a hermit. A kingdom bought with the deaths of teachers, cousins and a brother he never knew is not something he can bear to rule. His brothers argue. Draupadi argues. Sages come and argue, and at last he lets himself be crowned. But the grief and doubt don't leave him. So Krishna takes him to the field, to the one teacher still alive there: Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows.
screen: `HE WON, AND WANTS TO LEAVE.` → `NOBODY CAN MOVE HIM.` → `KRISHNA TAKES HIM TO BHISHMA.`

segments.voice: The next two books, Shanti, peace, and Anushasana, instruction, are mostly one long conversation, and the peace sought is Yudhishthira's own. The surprise is who teaches. Krishna is there, and Krishna is God in this story. Yet he steps back. He gives Bhishma relief, so the pain of the arrows, the weariness and the confusion leave him, and his mind becomes clear. Bhishma asks, in effect, why not teach him yourself? Krishna's answer, in Ganguli's telling: he wants these words to come from Bhishma, so that Bhishma's fame will last as long as the world does. Then there's Yudhishthira. He hangs back, ashamed. His side brought this old man down. Bhishma has to call him forward and tell him he has nothing to fear. And God stands to one side. Many teachers read the scene as a picture of what Hindus call parampara: wisdom handed down, teacher to student, person to person. In the Gita, Krishna says this knowledge came down through a line of teachers, and tells Arjuna how to receive it: bow, ask your questions, serve, and the wise will teach you. Yudhishthira has to do exactly that: walk up, ashamed, and ask. Today, the person who could teach you most may be the one you're most shy to approach.
screen: `SHANTI: PEACE. ANUSHASANA: INSTRUCTION.` · `KRISHNA GIVES BHISHMA CLARITY` · `YUDHISHTHIRA HANGS BACK` · then, large: `PARAMPARA: HANDED DOWN`
